amendments.because: Listing every test in the new fix's Done-when duplicates next's lines and grows without limit; the fix names the failed run instead
amendments.done_when: When the latest nightly full run failed, forge next names the platforms and failing tests and gives the forge fix start command for them

done_when: When the latest scheduled run of a workflow failed, forge next names its failed jobs and every failing test, and gives one forge fix start command for that failed run (or the started fix's next step)

findings.body:
Gain 3, Work 2, Harm 2
Raise: Functional. If `Build & Test` fails and its fix is started, its stored why uses the unsuffixed cleaned name. When `Build Test` later fails while the first run remains red, this line adds file suffixes to both names. Neither alert then matches the first fix's stored why, so `forge next` offers another `forge fix start` for a run already being fixed. The proof covers two simultaneous failures but not this transition; that is distinct from the earlier collision finding.
findings.title: Not done: a later workflow-name collision loses the started fix's next step

findings.body:
Gain 3, Work 1, Harm 1
Raise: Test. The gh stub answers every call beginning with `api repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs`, and the proof checks only that prefix. Removing either `event=schedule` or the default-branch filter from the production request leaves this test green. In a repo with a newer manual or feature-branch run, that regression can hide the failed scheduled run or report the wrong one. No other test checks these query fields.
findings.title: Not done: prove the scheduled default-branch query

findings.body:
Gain 2, Work 3, Harm 2
The parser accepts only pytest-style `FAILED` or `ERROR` lines containing `::`. A scheduled Vitest, Jest or Go job can therefore fail with named tests while `forge next` lists only the job. The proof supplies pytest output only. This additional runner case remains open.
findings.title: Follow-up: name JavaScript and Go test failures in scheduled runs

findings.body:
Gain 2, Work 2, Harm 2
The request reads only the newest 100 scheduled runs across all workflows. A workflow scheduled every five minutes can fill that page in about eight hours, hiding another workflow's failed daily run. The coordinator expressly narrowed this case to a follow-up.
findings.title: Follow-up: retain failed daily workflows beyond the recent-run page

stop.reason: Coordinator (Harm 2, reversible): back to one GitHub request — recent scheduled runs (per page 100), newest per workflow id — so next stays fast with many workflows; alerts key by workflow id. A very frequent schedule crowding out a daily run is a follow-up.

why: A failing nightly full run on macOS or Windows is easy to miss, and Windows stayed red for days unseen
